opus-5.5.text:
I think "responsibly" is the right word, because the worst outcome is raising money on vibes and then discovering two years in that the core bet doesn't hold.

For me it came down to a few signals converging at the same time.

First, the formal verification side had matured. Lean and its math library reached a point where a meaningful slice of real mathematics could be expressed formally. That matters because it gives you a ground-truth checker. In most AI domains you're fighting over whether an output is "good." In formal math, the proof either compiles or it doesn't. That's an unusually clean reward signal, and it made me think the reinforcement learning loop could actually work here, not just in theory.

Second, the language models themselves crossed a threshold. They weren't great at rigorous math, but they were clearly good at the informal intuition part: guessing a lemma, sketching an approach, recognizing a pattern. The missing piece was grounding that intuition in something verifiable. When you see one component that's creative but unreliable and another that's reliable but rigid, the opportunity is in connecting them.

Third, I tried to be honest about what I personally knew and didn't know. Coming from math, I understood what research mathematicians do and where the real bottlenecks are. I'd also spent enough time around the machine learning side to see the gap between the two communities. A lot of AI-for-math work was being done by people who didn't care deeply about the math, and a lot of mathematicians were skeptical of AI. I thought there was room for a team that took both seriously.

Before I talked to investors, I wanted a concrete technical thesis, not just "AI will do math someday." Something like: here is the data problem, because there isn't enough formal math; here's how we'd address it through autoformalization and synthetic generation; here's the verifier; here's the path from competition-level problems to research-level problems. I also wanted to be able to say what would prove us wrong, and what milestones would tell us within a reasonable time whether the approach was working.

And then honestly, the people. I didn't want to raise until I knew I could bring in researchers who were genuinely world-class on both the formal methods side and the ML side. Money doesn't do the work. If I couldn't convince the right people that this was worth their careers, that would have been a sign it wasn't ready.

So it wasn't certainty. It was a credible path, clear early checkpoints, and a team that could execute. That felt like enough to ask people to take the risk with us.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I didn't decide it from first principles in some clean way. It came from spending years inside the problem and watching the ground shift under me.

When I was doing math research, the bottleneck was never ideas in the abstract. It was the enormous amount of time between having a hunch and knowing whether it was true. You spend weeks on a lemma that turns out to be false, or you rediscover something that was buried in a 1970s paper. So I already had a very concrete picture of what a useful tool would have to do. It wasn't "solve the Riemann hypothesis." It was "close the loop between conjecture and verification faster."

Then two things happened roughly in parallel. First, formal proof systems like Lean matured to the point where a large chunk of undergraduate and some graduate mathematics was actually formalized, and the community around it was serious. That mattered because it gives you ground truth. In most AI applications you have to argue about whether the output is good. In formal math, the proof checker tells you. That's the single thing that made me think this was tractable rather than a research vanity project.

Second, we started seeing language models go from being bad at math to being bad in interesting ways. They would produce the right overall structure and fail on one step, or they'd propose a lemma that was almost the right lemma. When you see the failure mode narrowing like that, you start to believe that search plus verification can close the gap, because you're not asking the model to be right, you're asking it to be a good enough generator that a checker can filter.

Before I talked to any investor, I built small prototypes. Not polished, but enough to see whether the loop worked on problems I personally cared about, where I could judge whether the output was meaningful or just plausible-sounding. Some of those experiments failed completely, and I think that was important. It told me where the real edges were, and it let me go into fundraising conversations saying "here's what works today, here's what doesn't, here's the specific reason I believe the second category shrinks over the next few years."

And I also talked to a lot of mathematicians, not to pitch them but to ask what they would actually use. If the answer had been polite indifference, I wouldn't have raised. The answer was closer to frustration, people saying they'd been waiting for something like this, which is a much better signal.

So feasibility, for me, was the combination of a verifiable domain, a visible trend in model capability, a working prototype on real problems, and people who wanted it. I don't think you need certainty to raise money responsibly. I think you need to be able to clearly articulate what you know, what you're betting on, and what would prove you wrong, and then be honest about all three.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between believing in a research direction and having enough evidence to build a company around it. You don’t need to know that every hard problem is solved, but you do need a credible path to testing the assumptions that matter.

For AI for math, that means asking: Can the system make progress on problems it hasn’t simply seen before? Can we check whether its reasoning is correct? And can that capability become useful to someone, rather than just impressive on a benchmark?

The fundraising threshold isn’t certainty. It’s being able to explain clearly what you’ve demonstrated, what remains uncertain, and what the money will let you establish next. I wouldn’t want to present a research bet as an engineering task with a predictable timeline. You can responsibly ask investors to take that bet with you, provided you’re honest about which parts are still bets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between believing that AI will eventually be very good at mathematics and having enough evidence to build a company around a particular approach. The first belief alone wouldn’t have been enough for me to fundraise.

For me, the question was: can we identify a concrete technical milestone, explain why we think it’s achievable, and design experiments that could prove us wrong? In math, you have this wonderful advantage that you can check whether a proof is correct. But that doesn’t mean generating useful proofs is easy, or that a system that performs well on a benchmark will necessarily help a mathematician.

So I wouldn’t frame the threshold as, ‘We know this is going to work.’ It’s more, ‘We have a credible technical hypothesis, we understand the biggest uncertainties, and funding would let us resolve those uncertainties.’ And then the responsibility is to make that distinction very clear to investors—to communicate what you’ve demonstrated, what you’re extrapolating, and what remains a research bet.
